summaries.example: Imagine you want your team to win a game. You know winning is possible, but you do not know that it will happen. You also care about winning. That mix of caring and seeing a possibility is close to what philosophers mean by hope. Hope may encourage you to practice, but it can also make you ignore facts if you pretend success is certain.
summaries.summary: Hope is an attitude toward a future possibility that a person wants. A common philosophical idea says that hope combines a desire with a belief that the desired result could happen. But philosophers point out that this may not explain everything. Two people may want the same thing and think it is possible, while one hopes and the other feels hopeless. Hope is also different from optimism: optimism usually means expecting a good result to be more likely, while hope can remain when success seems very unlikely. Across history, philosophers have judged hope in different ways. Some ancient thinkers saw it as a comfort or a source of courage; others thought it came from not knowing enough. Christian thinkers often treated hope as an important part of religious life. Later thinkers connected hope with fear, reason, action, and politics. Kant linked hope to questions about morality, happiness, religion, and a better future. Some existentialist philosophers criticized hope for pulling people away from reality, while others saw it as a way to resist despair. Pragmatist philosophers connected hope with habits, action, democracy, and possible improvement. Modern philosophers and psychologists continue asking what hope is, when it is sensible, and whether it helps people act well.
key_ideas: Hope usually involves wanting a good outcome and seeing that outcome as possible.
Hope is not exactly the same as optimism. We can hope for something even when we think it is unlikely.
Philosophers disagree about whether hope is mainly a useful feeling, a kind of thinking, or something more special.
Hope can help people act during hard times, but it can also mislead them.
Some philosophers study personal hope, while others study hope in religion, society, and politics.
summaries.why_it_matters: Hope affects what people do when the future is uncertain. It can give someone energy to practice, care for others, or work for a fairer world. But hope should not automatically be treated as proof that something will happen. Studying hope helps us ask how feelings, facts, choices, and shared goals fit together.

important_terms.definition: A feeling or attitude about a wanted future that a person sees as possible, even if it may be unlikely.
Wanting something to happen or be true.
A way of thinking about what might happen later.
The idea that something could happen, even when it is not certain.
A calm state in which a person is less troubled by fear and worry.

questions_to_think_about: Can you hope for something that you think is impossible? Why or why not?
Is hope helpful when you are working toward a difficult goal?
How is hoping different from simply wishing?
Can hope ever make people stop paying attention to facts?

summaries.example: Suppose a student joins a campaign for stronger climate policy while believing that success is uncertain and that the problem may not be solved quickly. The student still regards meaningful improvement as possible and treats that possibility as a reason to organize, learn, and persuade others. This is not necessarily optimism: the student need not believe success is more likely than failure. Philosophers would ask whether the hope is epistemically justified, practically useful, or both—and whether it leaves room for realistic criticism.
summaries.summary: The philosophical study of hope asks what kind of mental attitude it is, whether it can be rational, and what value it has for action. The standard account analyzes hope that p as a desire that p together with a belief that p is possible. This captures why hope is directed toward something wanted and why it normally excludes what one regards as impossible or already certain. It does not, however, clearly distinguish hope from ordinary wishing, expectation, or despair. Proposed additions include mental imagery, a special way of attending to possibility, an attitude toward external conditions, a feeling, or a disposition to undertake hopeful activities. Some philosophers instead regard hope as irreducible or as a primitive state with a distinctive role in thought and action. Hope also differs from optimism. Optimism generally involves a comparatively favorable probability judgment, whereas hope can concern an outcome that one does not expect. The question of rationality therefore has at least two dimensions. Epistemically, hope may be assessed by asking whether its object is possible and whether the person has adequate reasons for treating it as possible. Practically, it may be assessed by asking whether it supports rational ends, planning, persistence, love, or political cooperation. Historical discussions reflect wider views about the future. Ancient writers offer both warnings about ignorance and praise for courage. Augustine and Aquinas connect hope with religious virtue, while Kant treats hope as central to reason’s relation to morality, happiness, religion, and progress. Kierkegaard and Marcel defend forms of hope that resist despair, whereas Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, and Camus criticize some hopes—especially religious or metaphysical hopes—as distortions or evasions
key_ideas: The standard account holds that hoping for p involves desiring p and believing that p is possible. Debate concerns whether these conditions are sufficient.
Hope differs from expectation and optimism. A person may hope for an extremely improbable outcome without expecting it.
The despair objection says that identical beliefs and desires may occur in both hope and despair, so an additional feature may be required, such as attention, imagery, or a hopeful activity.
Theoretical rationality concerns whether an outcome is possible and whether belief in its possibility is justified. Practical rationality concerns whether hope supports worthwhile action or ends.
Historical evaluations vary. Seneca links hope with fear and anxiety, Aquinas presents different forms of hope, and Kant connects hope with morality, religion, and human progress.
In politics, hope can motivate collective action and support solidarity, but it may also encourage wishful thinking, unrealistic goals, or acceptance of injustice.
summaries.why_it_matters: Hope can shape agency when evidence is incomplete. It may sustain action where certainty is unavailable, including personal projects and collective efforts for justice. Yet hope can impose costs by directing attention and effort toward one possibility while neglecting others. Philosophical analysis helps distinguish hopeful commitment from mere confidence, wishful thinking, or passive expectation.

important_terms.definition: A future-directed attitude that commonly combines desire for an outcome with taking that outcome to be possible.
The standard philosophical analysis of hope as desire for an outcome plus belief in its possibility, though critics argue that more is needed.
A positive expectation usually involving the view that a desired outcome is more likely than not; hope need not involve that judgment.
The part of a mental attitude concerned with wanting or being directed toward an outcome, rather than representing how things are.
The part of a mental attitude concerned with representing facts, possibilities, or likelihoods.
Reasonableness in relation to evidence and possibility, or in relation to whether an attitude supports good action.
The view that an attitude or concept cannot be fully reduced to simpler states such as belief and desire.
A political orientation that treats improvement as possible but neither guaranteed nor impossible.

questions_to_think_about: Does a person who believes an outcome is extremely unlikely still hope for it, or merely wish for it?
What could distinguish hope from despair if both involve the same desire and belief?
Can a hope be practically useful but epistemically unjustified?
Should political movements encourage hope when success is uncertain?
Is hope best understood as a mental state, a habit, a virtue, or a family of related attitudes?

summaries.example: A student hopes to make the school basketball team. They want this outcome and know it is possible, but they also know it is not guaranteed. Their hope might lead them to practice and ask for advice. Another student may want the same result and think it is possible but already feel that it will not happen. Philosophers use cases like this to ask whether hope includes something more than a wish and a belief.
summaries.summary: Philosophers have discussed hope as a way people relate to uncertain futures. The most familiar view says that hoping for an outcome involves both wanting it and believing that it is possible. This explains why people do not normally hope for what they regard as impossible, and why hope differs from a simple desire. Still, the theory may be too simple. A person can want an outcome and regard it as possible while feeling despair rather than hope. For this reason, philosophers have suggested that hope also involves imagining the outcome, focusing on its possibility, feeling a special kind of anticipation, or treating the possibility as a reason to act. Hope is often confused with optimism, but the entry separates them. Optimism usually means believing that a good outcome is more likely than not. Hope can remain even when a person expects failure, as long as the outcome is seen as possible and worth wanting. Philosophers also ask whether hope is rational. One question concerns evidence: Is the hoped-for result possible, and is the person justified in thinking so? Another concerns action: Does hope help the person pursue reasonable goals, or does it distract from better choices? The history of the idea shows no single verdict. Ancient thinkers sometimes treated hope as wishful thinking and sometimes as support against despair. Christian thinkers connected it with faith and virtue. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, writers examined its relation to fear, pleasure, uncertainty, and political obedience. Kant gave hope a major role in linking morality with religion and the possibility of a better human future. Later thinkers split between criticizing hope as an escape from reality and defending it as a way to overcome despair. Pragmatists connected hope with habits,I
key_ideas: Many philosophers analyze hope as a combination of desire and belief in possibility, but they disagree about whether that analysis is complete.
Hope can survive very low chances. This makes it different from optimism, which is more closely tied to favorable expectations.
Hope may include special attention, imagination, feelings, or a readiness to act—not just a wish and a belief.
Different traditions evaluate hope differently: some see it as misleading, while others see it as a source of courage, faith, or resistance to despair.
Kant connects hope with moral progress and the question of what people may reasonably hope for when experience cannot settle the answer.
Hope has political effects. It can unite and motivate people, but it can also hide injustice or encourage unrealistic plans.
summaries.why_it_matters: Hope matters because people often must decide and act without certainty. It can encourage effort, courage, cooperation, and long-term improvement. At the same time, hope can make people overlook evidence or accept promises that will not help them. Thinking carefully about hope helps us judge both its power and its risks.

important_terms.definition: An attitude toward a wanted possibility, usually involving uncertainty about whether the outcome will happen.
The common theory that hope consists of wanting an outcome and believing that it is possible.
Wanting an outcome, whether or not a person thinks it will happen.
Thinking that an event could happen, without being certain that it will.
A hopeful attitude that usually includes expecting a good result to be fairly likely.
A state of giving up on a desired outcome or treating it as unlikely in a way that blocks hope.
A reasoned choice or effort directed toward achieving an outcome.
A view that improvement is possible but not assured, so people must help bring it about.

questions_to_think_about: If two people want the same result and think it is possible, why might only one of them hope?
How is hope different from expecting something?
Can a hope be reasonable even when it is unlikely?
When does political hope help people work together, and when might it mislead them?
Do hopeful people need to act, or can hope exist without action?
